description: Biomedical Engineer, former founder, now Founding AI Engineer in Barcelona. I’m into autonomous medicine: using AI to help people when no doctor is nearby, from space to disasters and remote environments. Looking for people excited by the same problem: AI, software, biomedical, hardware, design. If this sounds fun, message me. Curiosity matters more than experience, lets win this!!!
summary:
On the ISS, a sick astronaut has a flight surgeon on the line and can be home in under 24 hours. On the Moon, evacuation takes several days and the link with Earth drops. The crew has to watch its own health.

Moon Care is health monitoring software for that crew. It gathers more than 30 health parameters plus a daily mood check-in in one panel: blood tests of real astronauts (NASA OSDR, Inspiration4), radiation measured on the ISS (NASA RadLab) and wearable devices' data. Every parameter says how to measure it, why it matters and what to do, and shows its source. More than 22 alert rules warn when a value is out of range, each with the origin of its limit.

When several readings point to a possible health issue, e.g. an infection, bone and muscle loss, etc., a voice agent guides the crew medical officer through NASA's own ISS Medical Checklist, word for word, records what they find and prepares the report for the flight surgeon. From this point on, the information waits until the connection with Earth returns, and the report can be safely sent.

The backend runs as a Moon server that works on its own and syncs with an Earth server whenever possible. 

Our team found an answer for what NASA calls Earth Independent Medical Operations. An open research topic that will be essential for sustained life in outer space.
details:
TRY IT FIRST

Dashboard (tablet and laptop): https://mooncare-ten.vercel.app

Crew app (phone): https://mooncare-4qo5.vercel.app

Code: https://github.com/adoviguerav/mooncare

Pick any crew member and enter the demo PIN shown on our landing page. The first visit can take about a minute while the server wakes up. To see the emergency case, sign in as Amara Okafor, the medical officer, and press "Simulate a possible infection".

On Earth, when you feel ill you book an appointment, go to the emergency room or call an ambulance. On the International Space Station it is not so different, because a flight surgeon on the ground follows the crew in real time and a sick astronaut can be home in under 24 hours. On the Moon, however, that safety net is gone. Evacuation takes 3 to 11 days, and at the lunar South Pole, where Artemis IV is planned to land, Earth is visible only half of each month, so there are periods with no communication at all. From Mars, a message would take up to 20 minutes each way.

NASA has a name for what these missions need: Earth Independent Medical Operations (EIMO), which means moving medical care from Earth to the crew as missions get farther away. It is still an open problem (Human Research Program gap Medical-701), and NASA's Human System Risk Board already rates the crew having to solve problems alone as a red risk for short stays on the lunar surface. On top of that, the person in charge of health on board, the crew medical officer, is usually not a doctor but someone with about 60 hours of medical training. Today almost the whole chain (monitor, diagnose, decide, treat) happens on Earth, and that is why Moon Care starts from one question: which of those steps must keep working on board when Earth cannot help?

To answer it, picture a normal morning on a lunar base. You wake up and open Moon Care, as you do every day, and one panel gathers what your watch, the blood analyser and the sensors of the base have recorded: how you slept, how your heart is doing, how much radiation the habitat received. Since you are an engineer and not a doctor, nothing assumes you know medicine. Each of the 35 parameters explains in plain words how to measure it, why it matters, what is normal and what to do, and it keeps its history over months, because on a long mission the slow changes are the dangerous ones. A body map shows the same readings by body system, and if you want to understand more, seven parameters have short study notes with drawings and sources.

Before starting the day you tick how you feel. It takes seconds and keeps a streak, and next to it sit hydration, a guided breathing session and an exercise guide. We kept this routine short and calm on purpose: NASA rates behavioural health and team work as red risks for long missions, and the crew already spends about 2.5 hours a day exercising.

If a value is out of range, the panel says so, explains it and tells you what to do. It does this with 22 rules. 17 of them have fixed limits, while the other 5 compare a reading with your own usual value (the median of your last 28 days), so that the alert fits the person rather than an average adult. Every rule also shows where its limit comes from, so anyone can check the science behind it.

Then, one morning, something is wrong. Liam Novak notices blood in his urine, and while he is still wondering what it means, seven of his readings move away from his own usual values at the same time: skin temperature at night, breathing rate, heart rate variability, blood oxygen, sleep quality, C-reactive protein and lymphocytes. This list was proposed by our team's medical reviewer. Any one of these readings alone could be nothing, but together they point to a possible infection. The medical officer and the commander therefore get a red alert with the seven readings under it, so they can see why it fired, and Liam gets a notice that the medical officer will examine him.

We chose an infection because it has already happened in space, and each time Earth mattered: Fred Haise flew Apollo 13 with a urinary infection that reached the kidney, and Vladimir Vasyutin was brought back from Salyut 7 in 1985.

At this point Amara Okafor, the medical officer, has to act, even though she does not know the procedure by heart. She opens the guide, and a voice agent talks her through the Bladder/Kidney Infection procedure of NASA's ISS Integrated Medical Group Medical Checklist (JSC-48522-E4), one physical action at a time, while her hands stay free. She can interrupt it, ask it to repeat or go back a step. Meanwhile the agent writes down what she reports, such as the symptoms that are present, the result of the urine test and the drugs given, so the report for the flight surgeon fills in by itself.

Nobody on our team wrote a medical step. The instructions, the lists of symptoms and signs, the form and the drug entries are the manual's own words. The agent cannot choose a drug, give advice or fill a gap the checklist leaves, and the app only lets it move to a step that the current one leads to. The manual even has its own rule for a lost link ("In an emergency or during Loss of Signal, begin appropriate treatment; then call Surgeon as soon as possible"), and the guide shows it where it applies. In the end, the decision stays with the medical officer. When she closes the case, the report waits in a queue, and as soon as the link returns it leaves for the flight surgeon on Earth.

All of this rests on one backend deployed twice: a Moon server on board and an Earth server on the ground, each with its own PostgreSQL database. The Moon server stores the readings, applies the rules and serves the crew, whether or not there is a link. When it chooses to connect, it pushes readings and check-ins to Earth and pulls configuration and crew from Earth. Each table is written on one side only, so nothing has to be merged: Earth cannot overwrite what the crew recorded, and the Moon cannot change a medical rule. If a sync is attempted without a link, it is recorded as failed and nothing is lost, because the next one sends everything pending. User accounts are also pulled from Earth, which means the crew can sign in with no link.

Alerts, on the other hand, are not stored. The server computes them when the data is read (a reading that breaks a rule is an alert), so rules and readings cannot drift apart, and adding a new parameter means adding rows rather than changing the schema. As for the devices, the crew uses the ones they already have: a tablet or laptop for the dashboard and a phone for the crew app, both of them web apps.

We would rather tell you what is simulated than have you find out. The blood values are real: they belong to four astronauts of SpaceX Inspiration4 and come from NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSD-575 and OSD-569), and the glucose alert in the demo fires with the normal range that the NASA file itself gives. The radiation is real as well, the dose rate measured by the Lidal detector on the ISS, taken from NASA RadLab. Because astronaut vital signs are not public, the wearable and mood data come from volunteers on Earth (LifeSnaps). The 22 rules and their sources are real too, and one of them, VO2 max, uses a NASA limit from NASA-STD-3001. Likewise, the procedure is word for word from the NASA checklist, the voice agent really talks, listens and records in real time, and the Moon-Earth synchronisation is built and covered by automated tests against two real databases, although the live demo runs the Moon server only.

Three things, by contrast, are simulated, and they are labelled on screen. The first is the infection detection: the model is not built because there is no open in-flight dataset to train it, so the demo starts it with a button. The second is the seven readings of the alert, which are each crew member's real usual value plus a fixed change. The third is the link with Earth in the emergency case, which comes back with a button. Of all our limits, one matters most: the voice agent is a cloud service today, so without a network the guide keeps working in silence, with its buttons. That is why running the model and the voice on board is the next step. The six crew members are fictional too. Each one combines the blood values of one Inspiration4 astronaut with the wearable data of one LifeSnaps volunteer, so no personal data is used.

Put together, Moon Care lets a crew monitor itself, understand what it sees, act on a medical problem and document it without waiting for Earth. That is the gap NASA describes for the Moon and Mars, and the same design fits places on Earth where the doctor is far away and the connection is unreliable, such as remote communities, ships and polar stations. Most health dashboards stop at a threshold and an alert, whereas Moon Care carries on from there, from the signal to the alert, the guided procedure and the report to the ground. It guides with NASA's own checklist instead of generated medical advice, it shows the source of every number, and it is built for a lost link as the normal case rather than an error.

While building it, we kept a few things in mind. Health checks had to be short for a crew with a full day, and health data had to stay private between crewmates, except for the crew's immediate safety, as in the ISS crew code of conduct. Measurements had to be as non-invasive as possible, because they happen every day, and the app had to work for users with no medical background. We also wanted to be honest about limits. We found no open human data for bone, muscle and eyesight, the most severe effects of long missions, so their alerts are defined and waiting for data, and in the meantime the panel tracks exercise, the main countermeasure.

We built the backend with Python, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy and PostgreSQL, tested with pytest, and the frontend with React, Vite, TypeScript and plain CSS. The voice is an ElevenLabs conversational agent. The backend and its database are hosted on Render, the apps on Vercel and the landing on Netlify, and during development we used Claude Code as coding assistant.

From here, the next steps are to train the infection model when in-flight data exists, run the model and the voice on board, build the Earth view for the flight surgeon, load more procedures and add the parameters still waiting for data: bone, muscle and eyes.

NASA OSDR OSD-569: Inspiration4 whole blood measurements
NASA OSDR RadLab: ISS radiation detectors
NASA ISS Integrated Medical Group Medical Checklist, JSC-48522-E4
NASA OCHMO-TB-031: exercise overview (VO2 max limits of NASA-STD-3001)
NASA HRP: hazard of distance from Earth
projectRefs: LifeSnaps paper, Yfantidou et al., Scientific Data 2022
Inspiration4 data access through NASA OSDR, npj Microgravity 2024
Levin et al. 2023: ISS medical model and EIMO
